title: What has the world's deadliest venom?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a snowstorm joke about Atlanta's ten snowplows and a note of sympathy for flooding in Brisbane, Australia. They then cover scorpion venom research into cancer treatments (St. Louis University School of Medicine and Henry Ford Health System) targeting glioma brain tumors. They explain the difference between venomous and poisonous, then survey the world's most venomous animals: the box jellyfish (sea wasp), its nematocyst stinging mechanism, vinegar as a first aid treatment, and the Irukandji jellyfish. They discuss the LD50 toxicity testing standard and its cruelty, then cover the geographic cone snail, the inland taipan, how antivenom is made from horses, the cone shell's pain-relief potential, and the funnel web spider. The episode closes with listener Facebook questions on personal trivia.

entities.name: St. Louis University School of Medicine

segments.title: Opening banter and Brisbane flood
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Atlanta's ten snowplows and express sympathy for the Brisbane, Australia flooding that has killed about 34 people.

segments.title: Scorpion venom and cancer research
segments.summary: Two researchers, at St. Louis University School of Medicine and Henry Ford Health System, are developing treatments using scorpion venom that attaches to glioma brain tumors, which can then be radiated. Chuck mentions a acquaintance who underwent this experimental treatment around 2006.

segments.title: Venomous versus poisonous
segments.summary: Josh explains that the difference is how the toxin is delivered: venom is injected by an animal that makes it on purpose, while poison is passive, absorbed or ingested, and often created through diet, as with the poison dart frog.

segments.title: Most venomous animals and common guesses
segments.summary: Chuck guesses cobras, coral snakes, black mambas, black widows and brown recluses before the hosts reveal the box jellyfish, also called the sea wasp, as the deadliest venomous animal.

segments.title: Box jellyfish sting mechanism and effects
segments.summary: The box jellyfish can kill a human in about five minutes or less by paralyzing the central nervous system. Its tentacles carry nematocysts that fire venom when triggered by skin chemicals. Pantyhose reportedly blocks the trigger, and vinegar can neutralize the sting. Survivors may suffer dermonecrosis.

segments.title: Irukandji jellyfish
segments.summary: The Irukandji jellyfish, about the size of a fingernail, is pound for pound more venomous than the box jellyfish. Dr. Jack Barnes (unnamed in transcript) tested it by stinging himself, his son and a lifeguard, and all three were hospitalized near death.

segments.title: LD50 and measuring venom potency
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how venom potency is hard to measure and explain the LD50 standard, which finds the dose that kills half a test population. They note its cruelty, that it has been discontinued or criticized, and give examples like the coral snake and box jellyfish values.

segments.title: Other Australian venomous animals and antivenom
segments.summary: The geographic cone snail uses a harpoon-like venom to paralyze prey. The inland taipan's venom could kill 15,000 mice. Antivenom is made by milking snakes and immunizing horses, whose hemoglobin is then used. Cone shell venom is said to be ten thousand times stronger than morphine and studied for chronic pain. The funnel web spider is also deadly and aggressive.

segments.title: Facebook questions
segments.summary: Hosts answer Facebook questions about Chuck's facial hair, family reactions to the show, fears, deserted island food, the origin of the band name El Cheapo, how they spent snow days, and baseball walk-up songs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts direct listeners to the Facebook page, Twitter account, email address, and the HowStuffWorks iPhone app, then close the episode.
